summary.short: Minnesota HF 1370 (2023) creates a civil cause of action and two crimes concerning deep fakes: nonconsensual dissemination of sexual deep fakes (Secs. 1 and 3) and dissemination of deep fakes to influence elections within 90 days before an election (Sec. 2), effective August 1, 2023.
summary.long: HF 1370 adds three sections to Minnesota Statutes. Section 1 (Minn. Stat. 604.32) creates a civil cause of action against a person who disseminates a deep fake depicting intimate parts or sexual acts knowing the depicted individual did not consent to public dissemination. A court may award general and special damages, an amount equal to profits, a civil penalty up to $100,000 to the plaintiff, and fees, and may issue injunctions and a civil fine up to $1,000 per day for violating a court order; listed exceptions apply. Section 2 (Minn. Stat. 609.771) makes it a crime to disseminate a deep fake within 90 days before an election without consent, with intent to injure a candidate or influence the result. Penalties are up to five years or a $10,000 fine for repeat violations, up to one year or $3,000 with intent to cause violence or bodily harm, and up to 90 days or $1,000 otherwise. Section 3 (Minn. Stat. 617.262) makes nonconsensual dissemination of a sexual deep fake a gross misdemeanor, or punishable by up to three years' imprisonment or a $5,000 fine where a listed factor is present, with exemptions and immunity for interactive computer services and telecommunications providers solely for third-party content. Effective August 1, 2023.

notes: The document is the bill text (HF 1370). No session law chapter or enactment date appears in it, so enacted_by_bill is not recorded. The heading codes the new law to Minnesota Statutes chapters 604, 609 and 617; no existing provision is amended. Internal inconsistencies: (1) the non-consent mental state differs, requiring knowledge in Sec. 1 Subd. 2(a)(1) but 'knows or reasonably should know' in Sec. 3 Subd. 2(1). (2) The 'deep fake' definitions differ in wording between Sec. 1 Subd. 1(b), Sec. 2 Subd. 1(c) and Sec. 3 Subd. 1(b). (3) Exemptions differ: Sec. 1 Subd. 6(a)(4)-(6) add clear-identification and good-faith conditions and require the depicted individual's knowledge, while Sec. 3 Subd. 5(4)-(6) omit the identification and good-faith conditions and use 'knew, or should have known'. (4) Effective-date triggers differ: dissemination on or after August 1, 2023 (Sec. 1) versus crimes committed on or after that date (Secs. 2 and 3).
